title: Sensors and measurement
goals: Describe a measurement using its quantity, value, unit and conditions
Distinguish a sensor reading from an interpretation or decision
Use repeated comparisons to investigate a measurement problem without inventing certainty

prerequisite.prompt: A record retains only the highest temperature of a day. Can it establish when that temperature occurred? Explain using two possible records.
prerequisite.answer: No. A maximum of 26 degrees C could occur at noon or at 3 pm. The retained number does not preserve time.

vocabulary: A device that responds to a physical quantity and helps turn it into a signal
A value obtained by comparing a quantity with a scale or standard
An agreed amount used to express a quantity, such as a second or a degree Celsius
Checking and, when appropriate, adjusting a measuring system against a reference

blocks.text: A garden display shows 24. Is that warm? We cannot interpret the number until we know what was measured and the unit. It might mean 24 degrees Celsius, 24 percent soil moisture according to a particular device, or 24 hours since watering. The screen alone does not supply the missing meaning.

A useful measurement record names the quantity, value, unit, time and relevant conditions. For air temperature, the location and exposure matter: a device in direct sunshine may warm differently from one in shade. Record the conditions rather than assuming that every nearby device measured the same situation.

Measurement is a way of representing part of the physical world. It does not capture everything about that world. One air-temperature reading does not tell us how dry the roots are, whether a plant is diseased or whether watering is permitted.

lesson.title: Follow the measurement into a decision

blocks.title: Three different stages in a garden system
rows: Written rule checks whether value exceeds 28
Gardener decides what action is appropriate
An action or a decision to wait
blocks.caption: Sensing, checking a rule and deciding what to do are separate stages. A correct rule can still receive an unsuitable measurement.

blocks.text: The sensor responds to a physical quantity. Electronics convert the response into a recorded value. A later program can compare the value with a threshold. Nothing about this path requires us to claim that the sensor understands plant health.

The rule uses exceeds 28, so a reading of exactly 28 does not trigger it. At 29 it does. This boundary is a property of the written rule; it is separate from the question of whether the measuring device is accurate enough for the intended purpose.

Two devices are placed side by side in a shaded room and allowed to settle. At three agreed times, device A reads 20, 21 and 20 degrees C; device B reads 22, 23 and 22 degrees C. B is 2 degrees higher on every comparison. That pattern is evidence of a consistent difference under these test conditions.

We cannot conclude from agreement patterns alone that A is correct and B is wrong. A suitable checked reference can help investigate. We also need to consider whether the devices have different response times, resolutions or placement. Three comparisons in one room do not prove performance in every temperature range.

Calibration is a reference check, sometimes followed by an adjustment. Do not simply subtract 2 from every future B reading because these three pairs happened to differ by 2. A correction needs support over the conditions where it will be used.

Suppose one classroom device reports 27 degrees C near a sunny window and another reports 22 degrees C in shade. The five-degree difference may reflect the locations. Calling one device faulty skips an alternative explanation. First write a prediction: if location explains the difference, placing both devices together after they settle should reduce it.

A fair comparison changes the suspected factor while keeping other relevant conditions as similar as practical. Record what was changed and what remained uncertain. Repeated results can strengthen or weaken an explanation, but a short classroom test is not a guarantee about all future measurements.

blocks.label: Two devices disagree near a window and a shaded wall. Describe a comparison that helps separate location from device differences

lesson.title: Keep the claim within the evidence

blocks.text: A warning based on one temperature reading can mean the recorded value crossed a threshold. It cannot automatically mean a plant needs water. That broader claim would need different evidence. When a system makes a surprising decision, check the units, time, location, measurement and rule in order.

For classroom investigations, use teacher-provided records or ordinary safe room conditions. The reasoning task does not require heating devices, opening electronics or testing people. A clear paper investigation can reveal the same distinction between a reading and an interpretation.

blocks.label: A display says 30 without a unit. State two questions needed before using it in a temperature-warning rule

workbook.title: Repair an incomplete record
workbook.prompt: A notebook entry says 24 at lunchtime. Rewrite it as a useful air-temperature record by stating which missing fields must be collected. Do not invent values that were not observed.
workbook.answer: Keep the observed value 24 and approximate time lunchtime; mark the unit, exact time if needed, location, exposure and device identity as unknown or to be checked. A suitable completed record needs air temperature, value, unit and relevant conditions. Invented degrees C or shade is not an observation.

workbook.title: Trace a boundary
workbook.prompt: A warning rule is recorded temperature greater than 28 degrees C. State its output for 27, 28 and 29 degrees C. Explain why an off warning does not prove that the sensor is working correctly.
workbook.answer: 27 off, 28 off, 29 on. These outputs follow the comparison applied to the recorded values. A device could report an incorrect low value while the rule correctly stays off; measurement quality needs a separate check.

workbook.title: Compare without choosing a winner
workbook.prompt: At the same three times, A records 18, 19 and 18 degrees C and B records 21, 22 and 21 degrees C in the same location. Calculate the paired differences. What is established, and what further evidence would help judge accuracy?
workbook.answer: B minus A is 3, 3 and 3 degrees C. This establishes a consistent observed difference in these comparisons. It does not show which device is closer to the actual temperature. Use an appropriate checked reference, allow settling, record conditions and investigate across the intended range.

workbook.title: Investigate a new measurement dispute
workbook.prompt: A classroom sound display near a speaker reads higher than one near the door. A student declares the door device broken. Propose a safe comparison using normal classroom sound. Predict one result consistent with location explaining the difference and one result that would leave a device difference worth investigating.
workbook.answer: Place both devices side by side under the same normal sound conditions, using the same settings and reading times, or exchange positions and repeat. If readings become similar together or the higher reading follows the speaker location, location is a plausible explanation. If one device remains consistently lower side by side or after swapping, a device or setting difference remains plausible. Neither result alone proves a device broken; a checked reference and repeated observations help.

workbook.title: Limit a system's conclusion
workbook.prompt: An air-temperature sensor reports 29 degrees C and a rule turns on a warning. Someone writes The plant is thirsty. Explain the unsupported step and name information more directly relevant to deciding whether watering is needed.
workbook.answer: Crossing an air-temperature threshold does not establish root-zone dryness or a plant's watering need. Soil conditions, the kind of plant, recent watering and a gardener's inspection are more relevant. The warning can be correctly on while the thirst claim remains unsupported.

teacher.background: Separate physical quantity, recorded measurement and interpretation throughout. No hardware is required. Avoid describing every difference as error or every repeated value as accuracy. Consistent disagreement is a finding; deciding which device is accurate requires additional reference evidence. Keep units visible in both speech and written work.
materials: The paired-temperature table and two paper device labels
A sketch of a classroom with a window, shaded wall, speaker and door
Optional ordinary room thermometers used according to school procedures; paper data is sufficient
sessions: Retrieve information loss with the maximum-temperature prompt. Ask what time information disappeared.
Show only 24. Collect possible meanings, then build a measurement record with unknown fields.
Trace the garden diagram and test 27, 28 and 29. Separate sensing from the rule.
Pairs complete W1 and W2. Reject invented record details while accepting explicit unknowns.
Compute paired differences in the worked table. Ask whether consistent disagreement identifies the correct device.
Model a location comparison. Complete W3 and discuss what a reference adds.
Collect W4 independently. Ask for two predicted outcomes, not just a procedure.
Use W5 and the exit question to distinguish measurement from an unsupported plant-health claim.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Put the devices together, use comparable settings and times, allow settling and repeat, or swap positions while recording conditions. If the difference follows position, location is plausible; if it follows device, investigate the device or settings. For the exit: ask what quantity and unit 30 refers to, when and where it was measured, and whether that measurement is suitable for the rule.
misconceptions: The more stable device must be accurate
A device can repeatedly report an offset value. Stability and closeness to a reference answer different questions.
The warning proves the condition in the world
Trace the recorded number into the rule. An incorrect or irrelevant input can produce a correctly computed warning.
Missing details can be filled with sensible guesses
Keep unknown fields explicit until evidence supplies them. Guesses must be labelled as assumptions.
teacher.assessment: W4 is secure when it controls location or device identity in a meaningful comparison, keeps ordinary safe conditions, states two interpretable outcomes and avoids declaring certainty. If the learner only says try again, ask which factor will change and what each possible result would mean. Retest independently with light readings at a desk and window.
teacher.support: Give a record frame with quantity, value, unit, time and location boxes. Use a number line for paired differences. Extension: discuss why devices that round to whole degrees can differ at a boundary without either being grossly faulty.
teacher.next: Week 4 uses reliable recorded features to compare an explicitly written rule with a rule selected from labelled examples.
